title: Zipper: sidewall hybrid bonds join DRAM and logic edge-to-edge
idea: Random word 'zipper' forced onto die edges: plasma-diced DRAM and logic dies get interdigitated comb-shaped sidewalls carrying Cu/oxide pads, then they are pushed together laterally and annealed so the teeth hybrid-bond like a zipper. Side-by-side dies then talk through edge bonds less than 100 um long, with no interposer and no silicon bridge.
why: Interposer/bridge cost and beachfront limit; lateral die-to-die links at ~0.1 pJ/bit vs ~0.5 pJ/bit on a 2.5D interposer, and CoWoS capacity drops out of the BOM.

title: Lighthouse: lid-mirror free-space optical broadcast inside the package
idea: Forced link to a 'lighthouse': a VCSEL array at the center of the logic die beams upward to a curved, mirror-coated package lid, which reflects the beams down onto photodiode arrays on memory chiplets placed in a ring several cm away. No waveguides and no interposer traces are needed; each beam is a lane.
why: Escapes the shoreline/beachfront limit so 2-3x more memory chiplets fit around compute at ~1 pJ/bit over cm distances; removes large interposers.

title: Pneumatic tube: coolant microchannels double as sub-THz waveguides
idea: Mail tubes carry capsules, so the interposer's dielectric-coolant microchannels are shaped as rectangular waveguides and carry 200-300 GHz modulated carriers between chiplets while also cooling the HBM stack. A single channel provides both heat removal and a multi-10 Gb/s data path.
why: Long-reach (2-5 cm) chiplet links at <1 pJ/bit without extra routing layers; lets memory sit farther from hot compute and still be cooled.

title: Stethoscope: ultrasonic bulk-acoustic links replace TSVs vertically
idea: From the 'stethoscope': ScAlN piezo transducers on each thinned die launch GHz bulk acoustic pulses straight through the stack, and each tier listens with a resonator tuned to its own frequency (acoustic FDM). Vertical signaling then needs no copper via.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss); removes TSV keep-out zones and the TSV reveal/fill steps.

title: Origami: one folded thinned DRAM strip forms an 8-high stack
idea: Forced 'origami': instead of dicing and stacking 8 dies, a strip of 8 adjacent DRAM dies is left joined, thinned, and coated with polyimide redistribution that runs across flexible hinge zones; the strip is then folded accordion-style into a stack. Tiers connect through the hinges, so there are no TSVs and no die-to-die alignment.
why: HBM TSV tax and stacking yield; uses wafer-level RDL instead of TSV etch/fill and hybrid bonding tools, so capital intensity is lower.

title: Toll booth: HBM base-die-as-a-service, disaggregated stack supply chain
idea: The 'toll booth' is the gate at the road's entry, and the HBM base logic die is the gate to the stack. Standardize the base die-to-core die interface so a logic foundry makes base dies and any vendor's core DRAM dies can be stacked on them at a U.S. OSAT. The base die becomes a separately sourced, competitively bid part.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supplier concentration; opens HBM assembly to new entrants and moves the logic-heavy periphery onto cheaper logic wafers.

title: Rubber stamp: micro-transfer-print DRAM confetti into logic BEOL
idea: An elastomer 'rubber stamp' picks thousands of 200 um DRAM tiles from a released source wafer at once and prints them into cavities in the processor's upper metal layers, within 50 um of the cores, where they are connected by one RDL layer.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5); near-core memory at <0.2 pJ/bit with no TSVs or interposer, and tiles can be tested before printing for high yield.

title: Velcro: reworkable copper-nanowire hook-and-loop die stacking
idea: Forced 'velcro': dense Cu nanowire forests on both bonding faces interlock mechanically and cold-weld at room temperature at about 5 um pitch. A die that fails final test can be peeled off the HBM stack and replaced, which permanent hybrid bonds cannot allow.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30%; reworkable stacks could recover most of the scrapped good dies, and room-temperature bonding avoids retention damage from heat.

title: Sushi conveyor: time-slotted page carousel ring for shared reads
idea: Memory chiplets put pages onto a circulating, time-slotted ring bus like dishes on a sushi belt; every accelerator snoops the passing slot and takes what it needs. Shared data such as batched-inference weights is read from DRAM once and consumed by N devices.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth for broadcast data: N-fold fewer DRAM reads of shared weights, so fewer HBM stacks are needed per cluster.

title: Hearing aid: logic die reads DRAM bitlines directly through bonds
idea: Like a hearing aid amplifying faint sound: fine-pitch hybrid bonds expose DRAM local bitlines to a logic die stacked face-to-face, and the logic die's sense amplifiers resolve 50-100 mV signals directly. The DRAM-side global datapath, serializers and I/O drivers are deleted.
why: Periphery ~49% of die and I/O energy; interface energy <0.05 pJ/bit and maybe 30-40% more array area per DRAM die.

title: Chandelier: DRAM blades hung edge-on perpendicular to processor
idea: Forced 'chandelier': DRAM dies are mounted vertically, edge-on, like hanging crystals, with sidewall pads soldered to the processor substrate. Coolant flows between the blades, and 32 or more blades fit per package with no TSVs.
why: TSV tax and stack thermal limits; vertical orientation gives every die its own short edge link and its own cooling surface.

title: Loom: woven glass-fiber and microwire fabric interposer
idea: From a 'loom': glass fibers and 10 um insulated Cu microwires are woven on a textile loom into a fabric, resin-impregnated, and laser-opened at the pad sites. The fabric gives thousands of chiplet-to-chiplet links with zero lithography.
why: Capital intensity and CoWoS scarcity; could cut interposer cost ~10x, and textile looms are a U.S.-buildable tool base.

title: Magnifying glass: 1310 nm optical vias pass light through silicon
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so stacked dies signal vertically through the bulk with bonded micro-emitters, backside diffractive (Fresnel) lenses that focus the beam like a magnifying glass, and Ge photodiodes on the tier above.
why: Replaces TSVs and their keep-out area with optical vias; no copper reveal/fill steps and better stack yield.

title: Railway switch: MEMS optical circuit switching pools rack memory
idea: Like railway points: memory sleds connect over fiber through a MEMS optical circuit switch that re-routes whole sleds to whichever accelerator needs capacity, reconfiguring on ms timescales.
why: Stranded memory (often 20-30% in clusters) becomes usable supply, raising effective DRAM per dollar with no new wafers.

title: Ant pheromone: hot pages migrate autonomously toward requesting chiplet
idea: Like ants following pheromone trails: each memory chiplet keeps per-page counters tagged by requester, and pages whose trail strength crosses a threshold migrate across the chiplet mesh toward the heaviest user in the background.
why: Data-movement energy: 30-40% fewer mesh hops on average for multi-chiplet accelerators.

title: Slinky: helical micro-spring bonds absorb CTE mismatch
idea: Forced 'slinky': electroplated helical micro-springs at 10 um pitch connect silicon DRAM dies to large glass or organic panels and flex to absorb CTE mismatch, so large panels do not crack or warp joints.
why: Panel-level packaging cost; lets cheap large substrates replace silicon interposers for memory-rich modules.

title: Sponge: porous-silicon low-k trenches under long interposer wires
idea: Like a sponge: regions of the silicon interposer under long RDL lines are electrochemically etched into porous silicon (k about 2 vs 3.9). This cuts line capacitance roughly 40%, and the CV-squared energy of cm-long chiplet links falls with it.
why: pJ/bit on 2.5D links (fact 5): roughly 30-40% lower link energy at the same swing.

title: Choir: frequency-multiplexed mm-wave carriers share each TSV
idea: Like a choir singing different notes on one stage: each TSV carries 4 mm-wave carriers with on-die mixers and filters, so one via does the work of four.
why: HBM TSV count and keep-out area cut about 4x, recovering part of the ~3x area-per-bit HBM tax.

title: Card catalog: base-die Bloom filters answer misses before crossing link
idea: Like a library card catalog: the HBM/CXL memory base die keeps Bloom-filter catalogs of key-value and embedding tables, so a lookup that would miss is answered 'absent' without moving data across the link or opening a row.
why: Destructive-read and overfetch energy (fact 8) for sparse lookups; cuts 20-50% of wasted activations in recommendation and retrieval workloads.

title: Mosaic: wafer-scale DRAM-on-logic with defective tiles mapped out
idea: Forced 'mosaic': a whole undiced DRAM wafer is bonded face-to-face to a logic wafer, and tiles found bad at test are fused out of a mosaic address map. The result is one wafer-scale memory with no packaging, no PHYs and no dicing between memory and compute.
why: Interface energy and packaging cost; removes PHY/SerDes per die and gives TB/s-class bandwidth per mm of wafer.

title: Tide: lanes reverse direction as read/write traffic ebbs and flows
idea: Like tides: memory link lanes are bidirectional and are reassigned between read and write direction every microsecond from traffic counters, so read-heavy inference gets nearly all the lanes.
why: Bandwidth per wire, about 1.6x effective read bandwidth for inference, so fewer pins, TSVs or stacks are needed.

title: Echo: DRAM die backscatters host carrier, never drives line
idea: Forced 'echo': the host sends a continuous carrier, and the DRAM die only switches its termination impedance to reflect a modulated echo (RFID-style backscatter). The slow-transistor DRAM process never has to build high-speed drivers.
why: DRAM-side I/O energy and periphery area; transmit power moves to the logic node, which does it 5-10x more efficiently.

title: Umbrella: package lid delivers backside power, freeing TSVs
idea: Forced 'umbrella': the metal lid becomes a power/ground plane with spring contacts onto the backside of each stack die (through backside metal), so power comes down from above and the power TSVs, often a third of the total, are freed for data or deleted.
why: HBM TSV tax and IR drop; ~30% fewer TSVs or 1.3x more data TSVs at the same area.

title: Vending machine: per-GB-hour marketplace for idle cluster DRAM
idea: Like a vending machine for memory: a software agent on each server advertises idle DRAM, and a broker rents it to memory-starved jobs as RDMA-backed far memory (swap/tier) at per-GB-hour prices, built on stock Linux and RDMA NICs. $1M covers a 4-person team for 24 months.
why: Stranded memory (often 25-40% idle) becomes usable supply with no fab; effective DRAM supply grows 10-20% per adopting cluster.

title: Piggy bank: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn on CXL expander cards
idea: The 'piggy bank' of savings is the DDR4 sitting in decommissioned servers. Design a PCIe/CXL card around an off-the-shelf CXL memory controller ASIC that hosts 8 used DDR4 RDIMMs, plus a burn-in and test flow, and sell it as a capacity tier. Board design and pilot runs fit within $1M.
why: Cost per bit and supply: reused bits cost roughly 10-20% of new DDR5 and need zero new wafers.

title: Compost: e-waste DRAM package reclamation and reballing line
idea: From 'compost': a small line desolders DRAM packages from scrapped boards with IR rework tools, reballs them, screens them on a low-cost FPGA-based tester, and bins them by speed and retention for secondary markets. Equipment fits well under $1M.
why: Scarce-resource and cost per bit; recovers bits already manufactured and avoids helium, quartz and EUV use entirely.

title: Thrift store: buy fab-reject DRAM dies, remap bad rows in controller
idea: Like a thrift store selling flawed goods: buy partial-good DRAM dies that fail fab repair budgets at scrap prices, package them conventionally, and pair them with a controller (FPGA or CXL ASIC firmware) that holds large per-die bad-row and weak-cell remap tables.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer already produced, perhaps 2-5% more effective supply, at very low cost per bit.

title: Metronome: compiled deterministic DRAM schedule for AI inference
idea: Like a metronome: compile a model's entire memory access stream ahead of time into a fixed tape of activate, read, refresh and precharge commands that avoids bank conflicts and refresh collisions. An FPGA-with-HBM controller plays the tape back.
why: Raises HBM bandwidth utilization from ~60% to ~90%, about 1.5x more work per stack, so fewer stacks are needed.

title: Jigsaw puzzle: compiler packs tensor tiles to DRAM row boundaries
idea: Like fitting jigsaw pieces: a compiler pass lays out weights and KV-cache tiles so that each row activation delivers a whole tile of useful data and every opened page is read fully, guided by the DRAM's address-mapping function.
why: Destructive read and 128x page overfetch (fact 8); cuts activation energy per useful bit 3-10x on supported workloads.

title: Paper airplane: bit-plane layout so reads fetch only needed precision
idea: A paper airplane flies with only what it needs: weights are stored transposed into bit-planes, so a 4-bit inference pass reads only the top 4 planes of FP16 weights over the link. Implemented as a controller and layout change on an FPGA prototype.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth: 2-4x fewer bits moved per inference, and one stored copy serves many precisions.

title: Spare tire: repurpose ECC lanes as data for hash-verified weights
idea: The 'spare tire' is the ECC chip on every server DIMM. For read-only model weights protected by per-block cryptographic hashes at load time plus periodic scrubbing, the controller uses the ECC lanes as extra data width.
why: Bandwidth and capacity: +25% on existing DIMMs, and ~11% of installed bits are reclaimed for AI weights.

title: Kaleidoscope: link-level cache-line dedup dictionary at both ends
idea: Like a kaleidoscope's repeated patterns: small matched dictionaries at the memory controller and in the CXL device remember recently sent 64B lines, and a repeated line crosses the link as a 10-bit index. Prototyped in FPGA RTL.
why: Link bandwidth and pJ/bit: 1.3-2x effective bandwidth on zero-heavy or duplicate-heavy traffic.

title: Mailbox: CXL FPGA card does gather and filter near memory
idea: Like dropping a letter in a mailbox: the host writes a command descriptor to a mailbox region on an FPGA CXL memory card, the card gathers, filters or sparse-indexes rows locally, and only result lines return across the link. Built on an off-the-shelf FPGA CXL board.
why: Data movement: 5-20x fewer bytes over the link for embedding and graph lookups.

title: Abacus: accumulate-on-write memory-side atomics halve gradient traffic
idea: Like beads sliding on an abacus: the memory controller on an FPGA card adds incoming partial sums into stored values, so writes are atomic accumulate operations and no read-modify-write round trip is needed.
why: Halves link traffic for gradient accumulation and histograms; saves both energy and bandwidth.

title: Tetris: 32-byte sector fetch via burst-chop and sector-valid caches
idea: Like Tetris filling only the gaps: last-level caches track 32B sector-valid bits, and the controller issues DDR5 burst-chop or LPDDR short bursts so sparse accesses fetch half lines. Implemented in open-source controller RTL.
why: Overfetch (fact 8); 20-40% less data moved on irregular workloads.

title: Firefly: burst-mode memory link wakes from off in 10 ns
idea: Like a firefly blinking: the memory PHY powers fully off between bursts and relocks in under 10 ns by keeping a forwarded clock and stored equalizer state, prototyped first on FPGA transceivers and then on a cheap MPW test chip.
why: Idle and low-utilization link power: energy per bit at 20% utilization falls 3-5x.

title: Tattoo: aerosol-jet printed die-to-die bridges across chiplet gaps
idea: Forced 'tattoo ink': an aerosol-jet printer writes 20 um-pitch silver/copper traces over a printed dielectric ramp directly across the gap between a memory die and a logic die placed on a plain substrate, replacing silicon bridges. Tool rental or a ~$500k tool fits the budget.
why: Capital intensity: maskless chiplet interconnect at a fraction of bridge or interposer cost, buildable in any U.S. lab.

title: Fridge magnet: magnetic self-alignment for low-cost chiplet assembly
idea: Like a fridge magnet snapping into place: dies get patterned Ni/Co pads and are dropped onto a substrate over a patterned magnet fixture that pulls each die to sub-micron alignment, then bonded in a batch oven, with no $5M placement tool.
why: Packaging capital intensity; fine-pitch memory-logic assembly on cheap equipment and a U.S.-friendly assembly route.

title: Typewriter ribbon: revive tape-automated bonding for fine-pitch memory links
idea: Inspired by the typewriter ribbon: use modern 20 um-pitch polyimide flex tape (TAB, a 1970s technology) gang-bonded to memory and processor pads, giving wide, short memory buses between separate packages without an interposer.
why: Interposer cost and capacity; wide-bus links at ~1 pJ/bit from existing flex makers.

title: Garden hose: flyover twinax from package straight to memory modules
idea: Like a garden hose run over the lawn instead of under it: memory signals leave the processor package on flyover twinax cables to near-socket CAMM modules, bypassing lossy PCB traces, so DDR5/LPDDR runs faster at lower drive energy. Off-the-shelf cable assemblies.
why: pJ/bit and bandwidth of off-package DRAM: 20-30% less I/O energy and higher speed bins on existing chips.

title: Paperclip: clip-on backside LPDDR module with pressure contacts
idea: Forced 'paperclip': a spring-clip frame presses an LPDDR module onto pads on the back of the processor substrate, directly behind the die, through compliant pogo/elastomer contacts. Traces get millimeters long, and the module stays field-replaceable.
why: I/O energy and capacity flexibility; near-PoP energy with upgradability, so less memory is overprovisioned at purchase.

title: Toothpaste: stencil-printed silver-sinter micro-bumps for chiplet assembly
idea: Squeezed like toothpaste: nano-silver sinter paste is stencil-printed into 40 um-pitch bumps and sintered at about 200 C without thermocompression bonders, on equipment that SMT lines already own.
why: Capital intensity and thermal budget; low-temperature joints protect DRAM retention, and assembly needs about 1/10 the tool cost.

title: Tuning fork: resonant LC clocking for low-power memory PHY
idea: Like a tuning fork ringing at its natural frequency: on-die LC tanks resonate the forwarded clock distribution of a memory PHY, recycling clock charge instead of burning it, demonstrated on one ~$150k MPW shuttle.
why: Clocking is often 30-40% of PHY power; 20-30% lower interface pJ/bit.

title: Coral reef: electroless copper grows bonds between facing pads
idea: Like coral growing into a reef: dies are held with a 2-5 um gap over the substrate, and an electroless Cu bath grows metal from both pad faces until they fuse, giving room-temperature, pressure-free interconnects. University-cleanroom feasible.
why: Capital intensity and thermal damage; no bonders or anneals, and potentially reworkable before passivation.

title: Lego: double-sided commodity LPDDR around FPGA as poor man's HBM
idea: Like Lego bricks: stock LPDDR5X packages are placed on both sides of a thin, short-trace substrate directly around an FPGA or accelerator die, with 16 or more channels in parallel, using a standard OSAT build. A demo module fits within $1M.
why: HBM TSV tax and supply; HBM-class aggregate bandwidth from commodity non-HBM DRAM at ~1/3 the cost per bit.

title: Seed library: open-source memory PHY and controller for U.S. startups
idea: Like a seed library lending seeds: fund an open-source LPDDR/UCIe-memory PHY and controller, silicon-proven on an open U.S. MPW, so U.S. chiplet and memory startups skip $5-10M IP licenses.
why: U.S. manufacturability and barriers to entry; more teams can build memory-side chiplets and new interfaces.
